name: Cross-border scraping jurisdiction
blurb: Where collection is lawful in the model home country and unlawful where the data originates.
summary: Where collection is lawful in the model home country and unlawful where the data originates.

part_3_high_value_red_flags: An absolute exclusion for copyright, database right, or other intellectual property infringement arising from scraping or automated data collection would defeat the core coverage.
A violation of law exclusion that applies to any statute, regulation, or ordinance in any jurisdiction would eliminate coverage for cross border unlawfulness.
A privacy or personal data exclusion without a carve back for publicly available data that was scraped would leave GDPR claims uninsured.
A sublimit for regulatory fines and penalties that is too low or that excludes EU GDPR fines entirely would leave the insured exposed to uninsurable penalties.
A breach of contract or terms of use exclusion would remove coverage for the most common first party claim asserted by website owners.
A territorial exclusion limiting coverage to claims brought only in the insured's home country would exclude the very cross border claims this exposure creates.
A prior acts exclusion with a retroactive date after scraping began would leave historical scraping activities uninsured.
manuscript_wording_and_carve_backs: Add affirmative coverage for copyright and database right infringement arising from scraping, with a sublimit and a condition that the insured complied with robots.txt and did not circumvent technical barriers.

Carve back from the violation of law exclusion to cover civil liability for unintentional violation of foreign data protection or intellectual property laws, while excluding criminal fines and penalties.
Amend the territorial exclusion to provide worldwide coverage for claims brought in any jurisdiction, with defence costs payable outside the insured's home country.
Add a breach of contract exclusion carve back for website terms of use, limited to claims where the insured did not knowingly bypass authentication or paywalls.
Negotiate a regulatory investigation coverage extension for GDPR or similar authority inquiries, with a separate sublimit and no requirement for a formal claim to trigger coverage.
Remove or soften the prior acts exclusion by setting the retroactive date to the inception of scraping activities, or provide an extended reporting period for legacy scraping.
Add a contractual liability extension for indemnities given to customers or partners for scraped data, subject to the same exclusions and sublimits as the underlying policy.

part_4_program_structure_and_limits.bi_waiting_period: Business interruption waiting periods for data centre operations are typically 8 to 12 hours, but legal liability claims from cross border scraping do not trigger business interruption coverage.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.business_interruption: Business interruption coverage responds only to physical loss or damage to data centre property, not to legal liability from cross border scraping, so no additional business interruption limit is needed for this exposure.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.property_eb_equipment: Electronic data processing equipment coverage includes servers and storage used for scraping, with limits based on replacement cost of hardware rather than on liability exposure from scraping.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.per_occurrence_primary_excess_layered_pr: Property coverage for data centre assets is written on a layered basis with primary limits set by maximum foreseeable loss at a single location, but cross border scraping jurisdiction does not change property pricing or limits.

part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.cgl_primary: A standard commercial general liability policy provides only limited advertising injury coverage and typically excludes copyright infringement arising from electronic data and contractual liability, so the primary layer for this exposure is a dedicated technology or media errors and omissions policy.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.paper_basis: Claims made coverage applies because claims from cross border scraping often arise years after the collection event, and underwriters need a retroactive date and extended reporting period to manage long tail exposure.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.excess_umbrella_towers: Excess and umbrella towers follow form over the dedicated technology or media errors and omissions policy, with drop down coverage for commercial general liability only where the underlying policy does not respond, but all layers remain subject to the same scraping exclusions.

part_1_core_third_party_liability_exposu: Copyright infringement claims from website owners in origin countries where scraping reproduces protected text, images, or databases without permission.
Database right infringement claims under the EU Database Directive for substantial extraction or reutilisation of scraped content.
Breach of contract claims based on website terms of use that prohibit automated scraping or data mining.
Privacy claims under GDPR or similar laws from data subjects whose personal data was scraped without a lawful basis.
Computer misuse or unauthorized access claims under laws like the US CFAA or the UK Computer Misuse Act for accessing systems in violation of access controls.
Defamation or reputational harm claims if scraped data is republished in a way that harms an individual or business.
Regulatory investigations and fines from data protection authorities in origin countries for unlawful cross border data collection.

underwriter_wants_to_know: The underwriter will ask for a legal opinion confirming that the scraping activity is lawful in the model home country and identifying which origin country laws may still apply extraterritorially.
The underwriter will require a schedule of all jurisdictions where scraped data originates, including the volume and type of data collected from each.
The underwriter will ask whether the insured respects robots.txt exclusions, avoids circumventing technical barriers, and obtains any required consents before scraping.
The underwriter will want to know if the scraped data includes personal data under GDPR or similar privacy laws and what lawful basis the insured relies on.
The underwriter will ask about any prior cease and desist letters, takedown requests, or litigation from website owners or regulators in origin countries.
The underwriter will require details of contractual indemnities given to customers or partners for scraped data and whether those indemnities are insured.
The underwriter will ask how scraped data is used in AI training, whether it is retained or deleted, and whether it is resold or published.
